subtopic: PROVISION FOR AMENDMENTS TO FARMERS' CREDITORS ARRANGEMENT ACT, 1934

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 10, to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the bill provides
for four amendments to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934. All of them are designed with a view to improving the operation and efficiency of the act and to enable it to accomplish more fully the purposes which were in mind when the original act was passed.
The first amendment enlarges the period of a stay of proceedings from sixty to ninety days. It has been found in practice that in

Questions
certain cases official receivers have had before them for consideration as many as 250 applications, and in the nature of things they have not been able to consider them within the sixty day period.
The second amendment is quite important but, as I believe will be found with respect to the others, it is not contentious. As the act stands at present there must be a decision by the full board of review, and there is no provision made for the functioning of the board in the event of one of its members becoming incapacitated either because of illness or for any other reason. This amendment provides that in such circumstances two members of the board may appoint an ad hoc member.
A third amendment is merely to clarify what was originally the intention of the act, namely that the decision of the board of review shall be filed with the clerk of the county court or of the district court, as the case may be. There is an ambiguity in the wording of the act as it stands at present which might make possible the argument that it would be competent for a county court judge to sit in judgment by way of appeal upon a decision of the board of review. This amendment makes it clear that it is intended merely that the decision of the board of review shall be filed for purposes of record with the county court.
The fourth amendment is designed more particularly for the province of Ontario, although by its terms it is applicable to the whole of Canada. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Vancouver
Centre): moved:
For a copy of all applications for appointments in the Bank of Canada, and a return showing all appointments made, with names of appointees, salaries paid and previous occupations in each case.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MOTIONS FOR PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion as it stands in its present form is not acceptable. It would call for a return very voluminous in character, although, of course, to that itself there is no objection; but I can see no good reason in the public interest why a person who has applied for a position in a given service should have his name published abroad if he is not appointed. It seems to me that the responsibility of the government has to do with those appointments with respect to which it has taken action, and in those instances of course the fullest information should be disclosed. I am speaking now with respect to those appointments which are within the purview of its authority.
So far as the appointments to the staff of the bank itself are concerned they are not government appointments in any sense. They are made by the management of the bank and I have no hesitation in saying with respect to many hundreds of applications that came to me they are not a matter of record with me at all. All I did with respect to those was to pass them on to the management of the

Motions for Papers
bank for such action as they in their judgment thought wise to take, and so they are not a matter of record at all.
It seems to me that the motion might properly be amended to ask only for that information which is within the possession of the government and with respect to those appointments for which the government is responsible. If the motion was amended to read something like this-for a return showing all appointments made by the government to the Bank of Canada, with the names of such appointees, the salaries paid, and the previous occupation in each case-there would be no objection.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MOTIONS FOR PAPERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much the remarks of the Minister of Finance, but I regret very much I cannot accept his suggestion to amend my motion, for this reason. Last year when the Bank of Canada bill was before this house and also in the banking and commerce committee there was emphasized at every stage by those of us on this side of the house the necessity in the one case of ownership, and secondly the necessity of control by this parliament over the bank. My question raises distinctly and directly the question of control by this parliament, and I submit that this house is entitled not only to know the appointments made directly by the minister or by the government but also to receive the fullest information in regard to all appointments made by the directors of the bank or by the oificials of the bank before the directors were appointed the other day. I think there is at least some element of control which should be maintained by hon. members on the floor of this house, and while I appreciate the courtesy of the minister in notifying me of his objection I must insist on my objection to any amendment such as the minister suggests.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: MOTIONS FOR PAPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion is not a debatable one and I do not think that the hon. member upon consideration will think that any government could accept it. It would require a very large staff working I should think continuously for months to satisfy the request now made. For some strange reason, as soon as the Bank of Canada was incorporated, various people throughout Canada wrote letters seeking employment in the bank. I received hundreds of such letters. It would be a very difficult task to get them all together. The Minister of Finance I happen to know received not only hundreds, but thousands of such letters. I think the total number he received was two thousand or thereabouts.
I have spoken to my colleagues and I find that they are in exactly the same position as myself, of having received hundreds of such applications. I am also informed that members received them and sent them in to the various ministers. In every instance no action was taken except to indicate that action would have to be taken, when the bank began to function, by those responsible for its operations.
With respect to the others, what the minister has said is all that could reasonably be expected, that is, as to actual appointments made, and the salaries paid. The government will have to oppose the motion as it now stands. It is not in the public interest and would serve no useful purpose to keep a number of people engaged for months copying letters sent in from various parts of the country to various ministers for the purpose of seeking a position in the bank.
Motion negatived, on division.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC PLANNING IN THE NATIONAL ECONOMIC LIFE
SCIENTIFIC PLANNING IN THE NATIONAL ECONOMIC LIFE
speechtext:
Whereas, in adopting the resolution moved in this house, which stated as its objective the
creation of a national council of social and economic research, this parliament has accepted the principle of the organized application of scientific methods in the consideration of economic problems,
And whereas, the conditions which prevail in this dominion and throughout the world, with the growing burden of debt, the general stagnation of business and the anomaly of wide spread poverty and privation in the midst of an abundance hitherto unknown, would point to the inevitable conclusion that the consideration which has been given to the adoption of those scientific principles should now be implemented by definite action.
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the time has arrived, and is long overdue, when a degree of well considered and scientific planning, on a national scale, should be substituted for the present practice of uncontrolled competition and unguided individual effort, in the conduct of the economic life of Canada.
He said: In moving this resolution at this time it is not my purpose to debate the question at any length. In the first place the resolution is largely self-explanatory and, I think, within itself, contains both the purpose and the reason of that purpose; and in the second place the purpose for which this resolution was placed on the order paper has already in part been served and is in the process of accomplishment.
It will be remembered by hon. members that on May 4, in the session of 1931, I moved a resolution asking for the creation of a national council which I suggested might be called the National Council of Social and Economic Research, and indicated as the objective of that motion and the purpose of that council the assistance which might be given such a body in planning the economic life of this nation, so that instead of the chaotic conditions which we then found and still find we might substitute a degree of order and correlation.
At that time the government did not accept the motion and it was rejected. I moved the same motion in identical terms in the session of 1932, and at that time it met with a more sympathetic reception and was accepted by the government, conditionally, and by the house, the condition being that this should not be immediately set up but that sympathetic consideration should be given to the idea and to the purpose, with the possibility and prospect of future action. I waited then for two years, and last session there stood upon the order paper in my name a resolu-

Social and Economic Research
tion couched in the same terms as that which I am moving to-day. Owing to sickness I was absent from the house at the time the matter came up so that the resolution was not proceeded with and it was dropped. I again placed it on the order paper for this session, and I may say at once that it was put on the order paper prior to the public announcements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and prior to the statement made over the radio and embodied in the speech from the tlirone that such a council was in the government program for this session and would be created.
I feel however, and it has been suggested to me, that it might be well to place this resolution squarely before the house with the issue involved, not the issue of the creation of an economic council, but the issue as between well considered national planning on the one hand and uncontrolled private initiative and competition on the other.
I believe this is a question which is agitating the minds of the public at the present time and I think it is a matter in which this parliament should give the lead. I feel therefore that I should be derelict in my duty if I allowed this matter to drop without giving parliament an opportunity of making a pronouncement upon what I conceive to be a most important principle and one having a direct bearing not only upon the situation in the country but upon the program which has been presented for our consideration during this session.
In discussing such a matter I think we must accept certain principles as being involved and inevitably involved in this resolution, and the first is this: the right of the state-and when I use the term "state" I am using it in its widest sense-to indicate the rights of the men, women and children within the confines of Canada who constitute the state, its right to lay down the general rules, to enforce the general principles and regulations under which private business, private industry and individuals shall operate; that the activities of individuals, private business and groups of citizens must in the final analysis be subordinated to the best good and to the real interest of the state itself; and1 that not only has the state that right but that right carries with it the definite power and responsibility of controlling to the degree necessary the activities of its individual citizens, of en-02582-214
couraging those activities which are beneficial in their application to the state, beneficial to society as a whole, to the men, women and children who live within this country to the state, and of discouraging and either controlling by regulation or prohibiting by law those activities which, while possibly profitable to the individual, are antisocial in their effects so far as the general weal of the state is concerned. I believe that is a principle which should be accepted by the house. It is one which, if applied wisely and intelligently, would assist us in dealing with the problems which beset this country and in bringing to a happy conclusion the troubles which beset the state.
I shall not suggest the personnel or the definite functioning of this body. I can only say this, that I welcome with gratification the announcement by the government that such a body will be created. It has been suggested during the course of various discussions that the government in its program has, to use the term already employed in this house, stolen the thunder or stolen the platform of other bodies. May I say this at once, speaking for myself and I think for my immediate associates, that we do not look upon the matter in that light. We view with pleasure, we receive with gratification the announcement that policies in which we have believed, ideas which we have enunciated, have been accepted by that body which alone is competent to put those policies into effect. We feel that our objective has largely been accomplished when that has been done and that success has crowned our efforts. It matters not to me whether this is done and those ideas accepted by the government now in power or by any other government so long as they are accepted by that body which is competent to give effect to those opinions and principles.
It is unnecessary for me to outline to the house or to the country the conditions which make such a course of planning necessary. The effects of not only the last four or five years but of preceding years which led inevitably to the conditions which we now find, prove beyond a doubt and far more definitely than any words of mine can do our need of some controlling authority and some intelligent guidance. It is not suggested that it would be necessary in following such a course to shackle, confine and regiment the individual initiative of the people of this country; but

Social and, Economic Research
it is suggested that all of those various activities which together make up the business and economic life of the state, should not be considered as individual units functioning only for themselves independent and thoughtless of all other interests, but should be looked upon in their true light, that of units within a body which is composed of all those units and their effectiveness should be judged not by the peculiar profits made within that particular line of activity but by the manner in which they may be coordinated and correlated with all other activities to produce a state within which the people of the country shall have an opportunity of enjoying to the fullest extent possible the productive capacity of that country; that they shall be servants and not masters of the community in which they reside.
It has been suggested and suggested more than once that if central planning of any kind were carried into effect it would destroy not only the initiative but the intelligent guidance given by those individual citizens. In answer to that suggestion I need only call to the attention of the house that that unguided effort, admirable though its motives may have been, admirable in many cases through the efficiency of those engaged in that unguided effort may have been, has resulted not in the good which was anticipated but in a degree of chaos, disorder and dissatisfaction which no one would desire to see within a country so endowed by nature as is Canada.
I shall not' presume to suggest to the government the form of that council; nor in suggesting that such a body may be of great assistance am I in any way detracting from the ability, sincerity or desire to be of service attributable to every government, not only as at present composed but to any government which may succeed it; but I am suggesting that in the very nature of things it is impossible for any prime minister or any executive cabinet, involved, immersed as they are from day to day in their tasks and meeting as they must do, demands upon their time and energy, to devote that thought, that intensive study to the correlation of the various activities within this country which in my opinion is essential. Further-and I think I may suggest this without offense-no matter how a government may be constituted, under what party or under what name, no government will claim that within its own executive ranks will be found all the brains, intelligence and talent of the country itself. I think it will be admitted by everyone that valuable aid may be given, valuable service rendered
[Mr. Speakroan.l
if to the assistance of that government, whatever it may be, may be called the best brains within the country and outside the government to advise and assist it in its great task.
As I stated, the resolution is self-explanatory. The principle involved is clear and distinct and if I may conclude by repeating my first observation, it is the definite assertion of the principle of the right of the state to lay down to all its citizens the rules, orders, regulations under which they shall function in the best interests of the state as opposed to the philosophy of thought that believes that out of uncontrolled private initiative, out of uncontrolled competition, out of the turmoil and chaos thus created, will eventually emerge in some miraculous manner the perfect state and the greatest happiness to the greatest number.

subtopic: SCIENTIFIC PLANNING IN THE NATIONAL ECONOMIC LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) introduced his motion in 1932 for the appointment of an economic council I had the pleasure of supporting it. And to-day I have the pleasure of supporting in a general way the resolution proposed by the hon. member. I believe it was Abraham Lincoln who said that "if we could first know where we are and whither we are tending we could better judge what to do and how to do it." Those words, used by the great emancipator seventy-five or eighty years ago, are just as applicable to-day. I received yesterday from Washington a report of a committee on economic security, appointed by the president of the United States to report to him. In this report I see on the first page a paragraph that I believe is worth quoting. The letter of transmittal is signed by the present Secretary of Labour, Miss Frances Perkins. It begins:
Dear Mr. President:
In your message of June 8, 1934 to the congress you directed attention to certain fundamental objectives in the great task of reconstruction; an indistinguishable and essential aspect of the immediate task of recovery.
And it goes on to say that:
Among our objectives I place the security of the men, women, and children of the nation first.
To my way of thinking any plan for this country's planned welfare must put the security of men, women and children first. To continue:
This security for the individual and for the family concerns itself primarily with three factors. People want decent homes to live in; they want to locate them where they can engage in productive work; and they want some

Social and Economic Research
safeguard against misfortunes -which cannot be wholly eliminated in this man-made world of ours.
Now, as a follower of this government I am very glad to say that I believe the legislation in hand or projected by it covers those three factors. Earlier in this session we had a discussion on the subject of homes. Anyone who travels across this country visiting our great cities, will find in them many homes not fit for human beings to live in, and not in large cities only but in our towns and villages and hamlets as well. I hope that the resolution moved earlier in the session in reference to the building of houses, and I believe more or less concurred in by all groups in the house, will be carried out.
In reference to productive work I will speak in a moment. As to safeguards against misfortunes that cannot be wholly eliminated, the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) yesterday, and supported, I believe, in principle in any event, by all parties, namely the resolution and later the bill on unemployment insurance, along with other bills which may be introduced later- although perhaps I have no right to speak of them, at present, will go a long way towards relieving the misfortunes under which the workers now suffer.
When this resolution was before the house on an earlier occasion I believe I said that it was in 1881 that the German Chancellor of that date, Prince Bismarck, first introduced the principle of an economic council and national planning. Germany herself did not do much with that until 1919 when in framing the German constitution at Weimar they incorporated in it that principle. Thereafter some seven or eight other European nations followed in line.
About the time of my visit to the old country in 1928, a special convention of the Liberal party of Great Britain had been planned to meet in Kingsway Hall, London, to discuss the question of industrial planning for that country. I discussed with several great manufacturers there and leaders of labour the subjects that were to come up at the meeting, which took place after I left England. That council was to consider national plans, not only for England but for all parts of the empire that are directed from Downing street. I find in a report of that council many recommendations, one being that a national economic council should be established, and another that a ministry of industry be established, and a council of industry consisting of 'twenty-five members. The report goes on to review the necessity for such a council and ministry, not to interfere with industry but to assist in developing it.
In 1931 the United States government also appointed a committee on this matter. I had the pleasure of visiting Washington to discuss with those associated with the committee their proposals. I will read one or two paragraphs in the report in reference to remarks made by the present Secretary of Labour at Washington, which I think are of interest in the present discussion. After all, any plan that any country is to use should include planning for work and for the proper housing and maintenance of the working classes. The present Secretary, Miss Perkins, then a witness before the committee, said:
A system of public employment exchanges would' assist us in organizing our labour market, and knowing where we needed to put the public works; people who had been longshoremen, for instance, could be sent into this pick and shovel work, and we would be in a position to take care of others at points where we would have to develop workshops. It would enable us, even in the midst of the depression, to take the best possible advantage of all the jobs there are.
In the operation of the unemployment insurance act in England they have divided the country into districts on a national planning scheme, with the purpose of providing employment in many districts. Miss Perkins describes that scheme in these words:
The English system is really excellent. In that little country they have 417 principal offices and 700 branches scattered over the country. So every market town has its branch employment agency and knows the needs of that particular locality. That is what has made it possible for the English to drain what they call their depressed areas.
We heard from the Prime Minister last night something of what is already planned by the government, and I congratulate them on it.
Before that committee in Washington many able and outstanding men in industry, finance and commerce appeared, one of whom was Henry I. Harriman, and he is quoted as saying, speaking as an individual:
I feel that if there had been in existence an economic council having the respect of the country, it would have been its duty to have pointed out the excess of speculation in 1928 and 1929, and the dangers of it, and the inevitable collapse that would follow such excessive speculation.
Whether that comes under a planning scheme I d'o not know, but certainly there should be some means of preventing what, took place in 1928 and 1929 in regard to speculation. He continues:
I think there should be set up a refe.tively-small economic council.
Social and Economic Research

And further on:
I believe that the council should be appointed by business and supported by business and should be, at the time, at any rate, purely advisory in its character, depending upon the type of men and on the character of its staff for its standing before the country. The problems that it will deal with are fundamental and underlying economic problems of the country, economic and business in their character.
The result of that very exhaustive inquiry into national planning is contained in a few resolutions which I will not take time to read. Reference is made to an examination of the natural resources of the country, as to how they can be best developed and in what association they should be developed. Reference is made also to the location of plants, many of which are located at points far removed from the best transportation facilities in regard to either raw products or the finished article. To my mind the result of the deliberations of that committee will have a beneficial effect on industry and employment in the United States, and I have no doubt that if Canada planned along similiar lines the benefit to employment and industry in this country would be equally great. The American Federation of Labour, at its convention in Vancouver, also endorsed the principle of economic national planning, and I believe it is high time that something should foe done in the way of national planning in connection with industry.
Many hon. members are acquainted with the tremendous advances that have been made in Russia. I am not one of those who decry the efforts of the Russians in any shape or form; I am willing to give them credit for anything they have done in the way of providing employment in their country. They have departed, of course, to a considerable extent from their first theory that there should be no increased compensation for ability. To-day in Russia ability is recompensed to an extent, though perhaps not to as great an extent as was the case before the Soviet republic was formed. They have established at Magnetogorsk a tremendous concentration of steel and iron production that must be considered not only by Canada but by the world in general. That concentration of productivity covers twenty-five square miles. They have built a dam 3,500 feet long and 38 feet high across the Ural river, and they develop several hundred thousand horse power. The operation of the plant requires approximately 25,000 tons of material daily. They have eight batteries of coke ovens, each producing a thousand tons daily. To-day
(Mr. MacNicol.]
they produce 2,600,000 ingots of steel per year. I have 'been associated with the iron industry, and through it with the steel industry, for many years, and I find it difficult to visualize a plant capable of producing 2,600,000 ingots yearly. At that plant they produce 2,100,000 tons of steel rails per year. We have two or more good steel rail plants in Canada; just fancy a plant capable of producing over 2,000,000 tons per year. They have three large blooming mills of immense capacity, with blowers that produce 115,000 cubic feet of air per minute. That is national planning, even if it is in Russia, and Canada will have to consider doing some national planning along similiar lines. Last year in Russia they produced 10,500,000 tons of pig iron. That was the second largest production in the world, and this year they are aspiring to exceed that amount.
All the planning is not in Russia, however; there has been planning in Canada, and what has been done here has been well done. A year or two ago in our own Department of the Interior we had a branch that planned for all Canada in regard to the development of industry. I am told that this branch is out of commission. Certainly it is not in the Interior department, though it may be tucked away in some other department. That little branch deserved a great deal of credit for what it did while it was in existence. It had something to do with encouraging the development in this country of the immense rayon business that has developed to such an extent in the riding of my hon. friend from Stormont (Mr. Shaver), and it had to do with other lines of industry as well. Our national research council is conducting many effective researches that should be beneficial, but in my opinion, though I may be wrong, their discoveries are not taken advantage of by industry to the extent that should be the case. I am sure that if all their discoveries were carried into manufacturing the result would be a considerable increase in employment.
Now I should like to refer to something that is being done in the city of Toronto, which city has had an industrial commission for some years. That commission has rendered very great and effective service by way of bringing industries to Toronto, thereby giving employment to men and women. The commission has been in operation for only a few years; I believe it was organized shortly before this government came into power. During the last four or five years that commission has been successful in bringing to the Toronto area approximately 125 new plants.

Social and Economic Research
I do not mean that 125 new factories were erected, but the new industries occupy 109 plants, either new or old, which they control. Sixteen of the industries sublet to other companies the manufacturing of their products. In these 125 new concerns, large and small, there are said to be employed 2,834 men, and the wages paid in one year amount to $2,822,000 or more. Perhaps not so much in the past year or two, but in days when they were making more money the great railroads had industrial planning commissions and undoubtedly they were successful in bringing many industries into the country, thereby providing employment. It is my view that if there were some way of coordinating industrial commissions, whether they be controlled by cities, railroads or other organizations, and bringing them under one national planning head we would save a great deal of wasted effort. Factories might not be erected in unsuitable locations. I have in mind a large factory which operates only at intervals and which so far as I am aware is not a financial success. It is forced to ship in its raw products to the plant location, and then must ship its finished product for hundreds of miles to the market for them. I believe if there were some system or scheme of national planning such as that advocated by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) we would be taking a step in the right direction. I do not have in mind any plan which would interfere with industry, because industry does not want interference. I was connected with it for a long time and I believe I know something about it, all the way through. It does however welcome and will accept assistance.
During the recess I visited a number of industries and I was in a position to see where national planning could be made effective. While during the depression Canadian industry has lost a great deal, yet it has benefited through its association with American manufacturing plants. Canadian engineers and managers have learned something through association with men engaged in the same occupations living in the United States. The result has been that to-day in Canada we are manufacturing many lines of machinery we did not make formerly. I visited a large plant at Dundas, in the riding of the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Wilson), a great plant operated by John Bertram and Sons. While there I saw three new machines the company was manufacturing. I have before me a photograph of one machine which is capable of turning out newsprint or rolled paper at the rate of 3,000 feet per minute, the complete roll being four feet in diameter and having a
width of 306 inches. By individual effort that company induced the American owners of the patent to permit them to make it in Canada for export to the old country. I have no doubt our tariffs materially assisted, and undoubtedly the Ottawa agreements were in their favour. I am told these machines sell at a price ranging from $35,000 to $40,000, and that already several of them have been shipped out of this country.
While going through many plants it occurred to me that if we had national planning in industry, where industries would not have to spend their time and money experimenting, we would be farther ahead. If there were some national planning scheme to ascertain what could be economically made in Canada, and an effort made to induce Canadian companies to make those products industry would be greatly benefited and unemployment lessened.
The plant of John T. Hepburn Limited is in my riding, and I believe that company is now making some twenty-five new types of machinery, iron and steel appliances, which were not formerly made in Canada. In my talks with Mr. Hepburn we have agreed that if national planning were widely developed industry conditions of employment would be benefited.
Since the beginning of this parliament we have on many occasions heard the expression "the new age." Certainly in reference to production this is a new age; I would call it a power age. One can step into a plant to-day and simply by pulling a switch put the whole plant under operation; by pulling another switch he may set only one machine in motion. Because of automatic thermostats and other mechanical inventions employment is becoming a very complicated problem and I am convinced some planning will have to be developed to take care of the surplus employees who are thrown out of work by automatic equipment.
While we have an effective tariff, one with which I am in hearty accord, I sometimes feel that national planning might continue from where the tariff leaves off. The benefits which we have derived from the tariff and trade agreements might be augmented by some further degree of planning. While in northern Ontario looking over some mines I learned about a large steel order for steel plates which was going to be given to a foreign country. Upon returning to Toronto, through persuading people I knew, I was successful in having the order placed in Canada. That one order meant 21,000 man-days for Canadian workmen. I wonder how many orders for steel equipment and equipment of other kinds go to foreign manufacturers that could just as well be made
Social and Economic Research

in Canada. If there were some way of planning to assist industries to obtain these orders I am convinced industry and employment wouldl be greatly helpedi.
National planning should be, as I said at the commencement, directed towards three ends, namely, decent homes, plenty of productive work and safeguards against the misfortunes of unemployment. After twenty-five years' experience in the industrial field I know that no line of national endeavour gives as much employment as is given by the manufacturing industry. Canada has four billion dollars invested in industrial plants and in normal times, through the brains and experience of industrialists, our plants produce about four billion dollars worth of manufactured products and employ approximately 1,000,000 workers. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from a large industrial centre where there is a large number of high schools and technical schools I wish to say a word on this resolution. The people of Canada up to two or three years ago have not been in the forefront of industrial and scientific research, and the result has been that Canada, with a population fifty per cent agricultural workers and fifty per cent industrial workers, stands far behind the mother country and the United States in its plans and methods of scientific and economic research for the benefit of the people of the country, although our problems are in the main the problems of these two great industrial countries.
This whole resolution is wrapped up with the question of research-scientific research, industrial research and social research, and with the main problem of all, unemployment.
For many years from 1921 to 1930 I brought before this house a motion for the appointment of an advisory economic committee for Canada which would deal with economic questions. In February, 1929, I asked the government this question:
1.	Has the government any plans for providing employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what are they, and what action will be taken, and when?
Again, in March, 1930, I asked the government this question:

1.	Has the government any plans for providing useful employment for the great body of the unemployed?
2.	If so, what relief will be afforded?
3.	Will the government accept the offer of the province of Ontario to provide one-third of the cost of certain forms of relief in conjunction with the federal and the municipal authorities?
I also asked in the same year this question:
What steps, if any, will be taken by the government to promote the effective merchandising of agricultural commodities in interprovincial, inter-imperial or in foreign commerce. so that the great basic industry of agriculture will be placed on a basis of economic equality with that of other industries?
I also presented to the house the report that was made by a special committee of the ministerial associations of the country, urging away back in 1926 and 1927 the appointment of a joint committee to study these particular problems. I quote from that committee's report:
Your committee is conscious that results will depend upon the birth and cultivation of a public conscience, which shall demand that standard of living in which no worthy citizen or his or her dependents shall suffer from hunger or cold by the operation of economic or other conditions beyond his or their control.
Unemployment is an unsolved but solvable problem. It results generally from the operation of forces beyond the direct control of the wage-earner, and constitutes a menace and challenge to every citizen.
Your committee believes unemployment contributes to the moral, mental and physical deterioration of our citizens, and involves immense annual economic losses.
Your committee believes the burden of responsibility to be a joint one resting upon all citizens, and in particular embracing the federal, the provincial and civic administrations.
I do not wish to offer any criticism of the government, Mr. Speaker, in this connection, because this particular resolution is above party politics. It goes to the very basis of economic and industrial society. The resolution refers to the necessity for scientific planning on a national scale. All industrial society in this dominion was built up in my opinion by Sir John A. Macdonald's policy of protection for agricultural and industrial workers, to provide work for our own workmen and our own markets for our own products.
Some years ago we established a national research council, and I think one of the main objects of that council should be to devise a policy that will provide a job for every man in this country by developing our natural resources, through research, and again research.

Social and Economic Research
The creation of a national research council is all right in its way, as I said in 1929, but we want something more. We want research, and more research, to solve unemployment, which is a problem that has been aggravated by the advancement of science and the inroads of the machine. As I said the other day, I believe that the Edwardian and Georgian statesmen must accept part of the blame for their failure to study the advancement of science and the inroads of the machine and its relation to unemployment the whole world over.
In the United States over twelve years ago, while our Senate was on holidays, the United States Senate-it is never on holidays but works just as long as the house sits-appointed a committee to study the problem of unemployment. That committee, presided over by a very able man, Senator Couzens, former mayor of Detroit, made a study the world over of seasonal, technological and cyclical unemployment, and investigated the question of the contribution to unemployment of science and the machine. Then in 1929 and 1930, when the depression began, the people of the United States had an organization, federal, state and municipal, to cope with the problem because of the efforts of that committee which had been appointed twelve years before. In addition they had a census taken of their industrial workers, and there was a joint effort made by economic councils and various public bodies to solve the problem of unemployment with which they were confronted.
Similarly, Great Britain twenty-three years ago established old age pensions and sickness and unemployment insurance. I just point these things out, Mr. Speaker, to show what other countries have been doing. For nine or ten years in this house I brought this matter up myself, and I was told I was preaching blue ruin when I pointed out what had been done in England and the United States along the lines I have indicated.
After all is said and done, it is far more important that the heads of our families should have remunerative work. Our boards of trade and the federal Department of Trade and Commerce for the last fifteen years have been publishing returns showing an increase in the country's wealth, but without showing how it was distributed. What has been the effect of modern machinery on unemployment? Every new invention that is adopted in industry puts men out of work. Women can mind machines just as well as men, and many men have been displaced by women and the machine.
I believe in fair play between the producer and the consumer, and I think it is the duty of all men to consecrate their powers of mind and skill of hand to the bringing about of a better social order for the common good and not leave it to the government of the day alone to drag the country out of the mire. There is no true liberty for the working man to-day. His whole life and that of his family are at the mercy of economic forces which are entirely beyond the control of the wage earner. We are taught by the Carpenter of Nazareth that God endowed men not for their own good alone but that they might be of service to their fellows, and in the parable of the rich young man he condemned the wrong use of wealth. Profit making cannot be the basis of a purely Christian society; the wellbeing of the community as a whole should be the aim of each of its members.
This resolution deserves credit for bringing the problem to the attention of the house. The other day reference was made to our high schools. A large number of the high schools and collegiate institutes of Toronto are in my riding, and it is most unfortunate to see young men graduating every June merely to lead a jobless life. They do not like to sponge on their fathers and so they leave home and go west, riding the rods, as it is called, in the fall; and I am surprised that the provincial and municipal police authorities prosecute these young fellows. The country has spent some four billion dollars in connection with our railways by way of subsidies and one thing and another, and these young men, who cannot get any work at all, are prosecuted when they ride on the railways in this way. But the question is, Whence come these young men? They come from some of the finest homes in the country, Mr. Speaker, but after they graduate from our collegiate institutes they are left to shift for themselves in a way that should not be tolerated in a country which is supposed to be Christian.
Something should be done by our national and provincial councils along these lines. Our councils of research, national and provincial, are now at the crossroads so far as this problem of unemployment is concerned, and I hope that very soon they will be up and doing; instead of inactively occupying large houses of stone and mortar provided by the country, I suggest that they should do something practical to solve this problem which is wrapped up with many of the other questions which this parliament faces.

Social and Economic Research
Take the universities in the city I come from. They are spending between twelve and thirteen million dollars on public education. Some of the greatest students in this country, coming from the Atlantic and the Pacific, attend the university of Toronto, bright young men. What are these men to do when they graduate in June, in electrical engineering, for instance? They go to the United States, notwithstanding the fact that this country has a potential horse power of 42 million, only one-sixth of which has been developed. If our national council of research were to take up the problem I think something might be done for young Canadians graduating from our universities and from the high schools and technical schools.
Technical education has been a great boon to Canada, but we have not considered the problem that arises from the inroads of the machine and science and technical education into the employment of labour. It seems to me that something must be done to take care of our university students graduating not only in medicine but in various branches of science-mining, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, civil engineering and chemistry. Why can we not make use of the magnificent resources of the country, using the talents of these young men to develop those resources? Take medicine, for example: Sir Frederick Banting and many others equally gifted were on the verge of leaving this country for the United States. In fact, the large universities of the United States, are to-day staffed to a great extent by Canadian graduates. One might mention the university of Pennsylvania by way of example; and we know that one of the greatest hospitals in the world, that associated with Johns Hopkins, has had very eminent Canadians on its faculty. For instance, Doctor Osier, a great Canadian, was at one time head of clinical medicine there, and he was succeeded by Doctor Barker of Toronto university. by Doctor Cuilen and many others. What an advantage it would have been to Canada had these great men remained in this country.
I submit that there has been no planning in Canada commensurate with the growth of the country. We have spent immense sums of money in connection with our railways but without any organized plan. A year ago His Majesty the King spoke over the radio and his words were indeed a challenge to all who heard them. We can learn a good deal from what he said on that occasion, because there are many reforms to which this parliament should devote its attention-reforms economic, industrial, parliamentary and constitutional.
(Mr. Church.]
Speaking again last Christmas His Majesty said that the world was still restless and troubled but that the clouds were lifting. We have our anxieties, he said, but if we face them in the spirit of one family we shall overcome our difficulties.
I do not see why our national and provincial research and economic councils could not do something that would help to pull this country out of the mire of depression, because science has affected1 the working classes very seriously. People want work; that is the only cure. The large corporations of Canada have been given a charter by the Canadian people, a charter carrying certain privileges, and those privileges invlove the assumption of corresponding obligations. They owe a duty to their creator, the public, and on grounds of public policy they should be made to fulfil that duty. If they fail to do so then the community, which has created them, will be justified in stepping in and adopting measures for their regulation and control so that they shall not run counter to public opinion and social justice.
Personally I believe that the new policy of reform will very largely meet the purpose of this particular motion. Canadians must retain their liberty and their dignity; they must declare for the corporate state; they must declare for the reestablishment of the worker's independence and for the principle of private ownership, and they must see to it that there shall be security for all engaged in industry. To this end we must have protection brought up to date, as Sir John Macdonald intended, protection for the benefit of the consumer, protection for the benefit of labour, protection based on principle and not on privilege. I believe the country is hungry for such a policy along the lines of Sir John A. Macdonald's principle of protection brought up to date to meet changed conditions and to march with the times in order to take care of the forgotten man. Such a policy will also establish a much closer union between town and country and much more intimate dealings and trade relationships between Great Britain and her great dominions and colonies than even the great Joseph Chamberlain ever dreamed of.
Such a policy will conserve our natural resources. It will give the business man a chance to function unfettered and afford him real protection from the abuses of competition and restraint of trade, from gigantic mergers and from hostile and destructive competition. The great industrial revolution in England was the work of seven or eight young men, some of them with

Social and Economic Research
no education at all and without any of the advantages of the youth of to-day. It sprang from the, very hearts of the people themselves where all great inventions, discoveries and great public benefits come, yet it changed the whole life habits of the people of England and converted that country from an agricultural to an industrial nation making it the work house of the world. I believe in such a policy for Canada. I believe the new deal which is enunciated by my leader is a progressive policy, a progressive policy for a progressive party. He said that the Conservative party would now dedicate itself to protecting the consumer and labour from the admitted abuses as revealed by the price spreads investigation, and would write a new national policy and a new industrial magna charta based on it along the lines I have indicated. It would be a policy which would rescue the workers of this country from an industrial slavery as bad as or worse than conditions a hundred years ago in England at the time of the industrial revolution. The rule and day of sweatshops and child labour unregulated has gone forever in this country, and so it should be with the scandalous minimum wages paid in some industries.
I belong to a group of people in this country who have stood up for certain principles in government and who have received much criticism in consequence, because I believe in fair principles as against mere opportunism in government-passing the buck. I remember once a little band of die-hards who were called by even harder names, the old con-temptibles, yet they succeeded in saving England, France and the world as well by their tenacity, faith, earnestness and high purpose ; and the Conservative party by its tenacity will likewise achieve its purpose.
In the early days of the people of this country, as I said the other day, we were a nation of property owners. In the days of Macdonald, Cartier and Brown everybody owned some property. The suburban or rural worker as well as the white collar worker owned a small home, small garden, perhaps a cow, a building or a small store. To-day, the rights of property have gone in this country; it is divided into a country of haves and have-nots. The whole means of production in Canada is in the hands of the few and the many have nothing. I believe the policy of our party will restore the rights of property in Canada. It is the politics of big business which has been destroying Canada. The Conservative party I believe is going to restore the ownership of property which is the normal want of a family. We have done forever
with the doctrine of laissez-faire and we must dedicate ourselves as a House of Commons to a solution of the question of distribution and restore the Canada of Macdonald, Brown and Cartier, Laurier, Whitney and Beck, when Canada was the land of the free and the home of artisans and farmers who owned some form of private and real property.
The day of die-hardism and laissez-faire has gone beyond recall. So has the doctrine of normalcy. We saw what happened to the government in the United States. The square deal of Theodore Roosevelt and the new freedom sought by Woodrow Wilson came to an end in the Harding administration. Mr. Hoover was a man of great ability and one who did a great deal for his country, but we have parted once and for all, and I hope all parties in this house will part once and for all, with normalcy, and consider a policy that will go back to the masses of the country and to the days where the political parties started in Canada, and that we shall have some help from the national research council and the provincial research councils and especially from the church. I have great respect for the churches in this country. I do not believe they have gone as far as they should. Prior to four or five years ago they did not speak out as they should against the exploitation of the humble worker. A hundred years ago in the days of the evangelical movement, the Wesley and Oxford movements, they wakened up the people of England to the conditions that prevailed. In 1847 Lord Shaftesbury introduced the first bill for the ten hour day and for the regulation of sweatshops and other business. Let mp in conclusion quote a few lines from Balleine's History of the Evangelical Party, in which he referred to the revolution in England of a hundred years ago:
The industrial revolution had produced a state equivalent to slavery among many of the men and women and children of Britain itself. The leader of the campaign to end the slavery of his own people was Anthony Ashley Copper, afterwards seventh Earl of Shaftesbury. "I am essentially and from deep rooted conviction," he said in his later life, "an Evangelical of the Evangelicals. I have worked with them constantly, and I am satisfied that most of the great philanthropic movements of the century have sprung from them." This religion he had learned from Maria Millis, a servant in the Shaftesbury household, who had been his nurse for the first seven years of his life. She taught him the great passages of the Bible; and so it came to pass that this poor woman was Shaftesbury's spiritual mother. Without her Shaftesbury never would have fought his fight for the emancipation of the workers.

Social and Economic Research
It is interesting to compare Shaftesbury's motives with those of his contemporary, Karl Marx, the founder and originator of what is now known as Bolshevism. Both men challenged the existing social order. Both pleaded the cause of the weak and disinherited. Both had a vision of a better world. But Shaftesbury believed in the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. He believed that all Christians were called to he co-workers with God in establishing the reign of social justice. His outlook was spiritual and his method persuasion. Marx, on the other hand, agitated for a class war; his creed was materialistic; his method was revolution.
As Balleine says in one paragraph:
It is difficult for us at the present day to comprehend the horrors which were rampant in England less than a hundred years ago.
It would not be difficult after reading some of the evidence recently given on industrial conditions in Canada.
It is difficult for us at the present day to comprehend the horrors which were rampant m England less than a hundred years ago. Lunatics, men as well as women, were chained in dark cells, flogged, dropped into water, sometimes half strangled, and even confined in iron cages. In the factories babes of five were made to stand on stools and feed the great machines for fourteen hours a day. In the mines children were compelled to push trucks through underground passages sometimes only sixteen inches in height. On hand's and knees they crawled through what was practically one long living tomb. The men who were placed over them were paid according to the amount of work done, and drove the children to their task with whips ami blows and other tortures. But women and children and lunatics had at last found their champion. Shaftesbury had entered parliament in the year 1826. After many years of labour and incessant abuse he saw his Factory Bill placed on the Statute Book in the year 1847. This great victory was the first of many in Shaftesbury's career. Throughout life he fought for the weak and the unprivileged, passing to his reward as late as 1885.

He (Shaftesbury) was a layman to the core; yet no nobler prophet of God is included in the calendar of saints. Cardinal Manning made no rash statement, when, after studying Shaftesbury's endeavours he exclaimed, "I feel that my life has been wasted."
So I say the resolution introduced this afternoon has not been wasted if it can arouse the people of Canada to do something for the high-school population and the industrial workers of the country, for the consumer and the labourer.

May I say farther, that I agree heartily with what my hon. friend from Red Deer said when he congratulated the government on its proposal to create a national economic council for Canada. No doubt the gentlemen who will become members of that council will

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the
hon. gentleman (Mr. Speakman) who has moved this resolution with his usual clarity of expression that as it has served the purpose of precipitating discussion, he should now withdraw it, for the simple and obvious reason that the general principles to which he refers are included in the speech from the throne, and it is contemplated that action shall be taken along the lines suggested by his resolution. It is true that the resolution goes a very long way, perhaps further than the speech from the throne suggests. But in view of the commission that was set up, and consequent upon the action taken by this house last year dealing with price spreads and unfair competition, I have felt some hesitancy in introducing tq this chamber legislation dealing with some of these matters until that commission's report is forthcoming. For the same reason I shall not traverse the ground to-day that has been so admirably covered by the addresses to which we have listened. I can only say this, that sometimes there is confusion of thought with respect to what is called scientific planning for a country. The raw materials from which conclusions may be drawn with respect to a matter of this kind are entirely different from the raw materials dealt with by scientists. The experiments carried on by those who dig and delve in the purely scientific field of research lead to conclusions that are definite, exact and certain. The materials with which men deal when they have to consider the problems to which this resolution relates may be said to be statistics gathered from many sources, and facts, events, circumstances, conditions. From that material men seek to draw inferences and conclusions. The soundness of the inferences, the correctness of the conclusions, may not always be apparent, in the very nature of things cannot be. But one thing is certain, that in this country during the last few years we have had sufficient experience to enable us to realize that we have not availed ourselves of the knowledge which we had in days gone by, nor have we arrived at the correct conclusions from the information we had. It will be recalled that we had a commission of conservation in this country at one time, and that an effort was
made to arrive at a definite statement of the conditions under which water power might be produced, and energy generated by which we might be able to increase the productivity of our forests, our mines or other resources. But it was found that at the moment it did not serve the purpose that was intended. The correlation of the knowledge that departments of government have is most important. For instance I can say frankly that not a week goes by that one does not receive suggestions from every part of this country. These suggestions are based very largely upon the experience of the individuals who write to us. They are experiences and conclusions that in many instances they draw from facts supplied by the statistical departments of various governments and countries. What is to be done with them? Are you to acknowledge receipt of them and dismiss them, or are you to give them that measure of thoughtful consideration which your time permits? Obviously untrained minds are not capable of drawing the conclusions that should be drawn from a mass of material such as we have sent to us from time to time. And as the mass of material increases, representing the views of this and that individual, based, as I have said, in some instances upon inferences drawn from known facts and in other instances without any foundation at all, you have a great mass of material that in my judgment should be considered by scientifically trained minds so that they might be able, just as the scientists test the material at their disposal, to draw inferences which the trained minds of men accustomed to draw conclusions from data of this character may be able to secure. But if it is suggested, as I do not think it is or has been by anyone, that a government should undertake to tell' John Smith how he should run his business, I think there is unanimity on the part of all of us that we will not accomplish the purpose we have in mind. If you consider John Smith as part of the population of the country, able to draw sound conclusions as to what should be done in order to secure successful results, then to make available the information you have to John Smith and all others I think is a wholly desirable function of government.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps it would be highly improper, in view of the action taken by this chamber, to discuss this matter for the reasons I have given, not only because the speech from the throne contemplates action being taken but because that action is delayed for the moment by reason of the fact that the price spreads commission has

Social and Economic Research
not made a report, and that commission is dealing with two or three very important phases, of the matters to which the hon. gentleman has directed attention. This house will have to discuss at a later time the recommendations made by that commission and the measure to be introduced by the government following the statement made in the speech from the throne. I do suggest to the hon. gentleman that the purpose he has in mind has been served, and while congratulating him and the other members of the house on the contribution they have made as to the value of scientific knowledge being applied to the nation and its affairs, as scientific ideas are with respect to the transaction of ordinary business by the various concerns carrying on the trade and commerce of the country, for those reasons I think the resolution might be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, to any resolution intended to encourage the formation of an economic council I would give my support, but in considering this resolution I must place upon it the interpretation which I feel sure was intended by the mover, and not the interpretation which has been placed upon it by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) or those to your right who have spoken this afternoon. I believe I am justified in placing on record my interpretation, and what I feel sure the mover will admit is his interpretation of the resolution. The resolution states:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has arrived, and is long overdue, when a degree of well considered and scientific planning, on a national scale, should be substituted for the present practice of uncontrolled competition and unguided individual effort, in the conduct of the economic life of Canada.
I do not think there should be any misunderstanding on the part of hon. members of this house as to just what that means. Hon. gentlemen opposite have interpreted this to mean the establishment of an economic council, which I do not think is the interpretation intended. I submit to the mover of the resolution that the interpretation might be expressed in these words: "That in the opinion of the house the time has arrived when national planning should be substituted for competition and individual effort in the life of Canada.'' I think hon. members should fully understand what they are going to support or oppose. So far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to support the establishment of an economic council on any reasonable basis, but IMr. Bennett.]
I am certainly opposed to the elimination from the national life of Canada of competition and individual effort.

May I say at once, Mr. Speaker, that I have no abjection at all to accepting the Prime Minister's suggestion that this resolution now might be withdrawn, particularly as the measure indicated in the speech from the throne will give ample opportunity to discuss and pronounce upon certain of the principles involved in this motion. I should like, however, for a moment to comment upon two statements made by the Prime Minister and upon one statement made by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken.
The Prime Minister pointed out, quite properly, that planning in economic matters differed very materially from planning in what we call technical science, and I can assure him that I fully appreciate that distinction. In dealing with matters of technical science you are dealing with factors that have known and tangible qualities which are unvarying and unchanging and to which, therefore, definite mathematical formulae may be properly applied. But we realize very fully that in dealing with human nature and human activity you are dealing with a factor which is unknown, which is intangible and which frequently varies, and that therefore we must always differentiate between the two forms of planning. I do not think, however, that this detracts from the value of proper guidance and proper control in the management of human affairs, which I conceive to be part of the duty of the state. Personally that is the attitude I would wish to take, and I believe it is the only attitude which would lead to success. You must consider all the factors and all the conditions and then do the best you can to bring about orderly conduct and orderly planning in view of those conditions.
But the Prime Minister went on to say that in his concept of planning while, with the mass of information at the disposal of such a body or of the government, you might assist John Smith in the conduct of his individual business by advising him as to the best course he might pursue, you must not tell John Smith how to carry on his own business. To a degree I follow the Prime Minister in this argument, but there is a point at which we must part company. I believe that every law we have ever had, every law at least inside and some laws outside the criminal code, is directed towards telling John Smith what he may or may not do in the

Trade with United States
conduct of his own affairs and activities, if be in the conduct of his own business runs counter to the best interests of the community as a whole. I believe that the state is fully entitled to tell John Smith either what he may or may not do in the conduct of his own business if that conduct affects beneficially or deleteriously society as a whole, because I still believe that society as a whole has claims which far transcend the claims of any individual within that society, and that in the final analysis the activities of the individual, that apparently may be his own interests, must be subordinated if they run counter to or conflict with the best interests of the people as a whole. So to that extent, if my understanding of the Prime Minister's statement is correct, I am afraid I must go beyond the Prime Minister in my understanding of the principle of economic planning.
Now I should like to make one reference to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury). He stated that his understanding of my meaning was that I would substitute central planning and central control for individual competition and individual effort. I neither said so nor did I intend to indicate any such thing. What I did say in the resolution was that I would substitute central planning and central control for uncontrolled competition and unguided individual effort. In other words emphasis was laid upon the control necessary in respect to competition when that competition became, as it frequently has become deleterious to the best interests of the community. I would guide that individual effort along lines where it might give the best possible service to the whole state. The resolution must be read as it is, and the wording of the resolution must be followed if my meaning is to be understood. I say again that uncontrolled competition and unguided effort have brought about the trouble, not individual effort in itself. Individual initiative is a splendid thing, something which has to be sought and encouraged, but it must not be left unguided or uncontrolled if because of the lack of guidance and lack of control the activities of the individual have a bad effect upon society as a whole. I would say at once that only when the activities of the individual run counter to the best interests of society, or only when the activities of the individual do not give to society the best service they could give, should society directly control that individual. When they reach that point the state has a right to intervene and to speak with effective voice.

On March 17, 1929, I had the honour of introducing a resolution calling on the government of the day to nationalize the supply of radium in order that it might be made

available for the cure of patients afflicted with cancer. Up until that time no real .state action had been taken with respect to the control and cure of that disease. Subsequent to that date, I believe in 1930, the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson who was then premier of Ontario formed a commission which was sent to Great Britain and other countries on the continent of Europe and also to the United States to study the question of cancer, and the application and control of radium for the treatment of that disease. As a result of the report which was made by the Ontario commission cancer centres were established. One was formed at Kingston, another at London, Ontario, another at the university of Toronto and only recently one has been formed in this capital city of Ottawa. Other centres have been established at various points in the dominion for the purpose of studying the control and treatment of cancer through the use of radium and other means at our disposal.
It is interesting to note that at the present time there is a campaign on foot throughout the British empire for the purpose of studying the cancer problem, a problem which is becoming one of the great concerns of the medical world. Subsequent to the time of the introduction of that resolution extensive deposits of pitchblende ore were discovered in northern Canada, near Great Bear lake, by the LaBine brothers. Those brothers came from a township in the constituency I have the honour to represent. Very shortly afterwards a discovery was made by one of the mining engineers in the Department of Mines at Ottawa, namely Mr. W. B. Timm. He, too, comes from the county of Renfrew; in fact his family live within a few miles of the point where the LaBine brothers were born. Mr. Timm was successful in extracting radium from pitchblende ore by a new process. That process of extraction has been carried on at Port Hope in the province of Ontario, and we hope and believe that it is going to be of material benefit in helping to control and cure the scourge of cancer and assist in the campaign which is being carried on at the present time with that object in view.
The first effort at organization in aid of the blind occurred in the fourth century by St. Basil in Cappadocia. Two hundred years later a retreat was established in Jerusalem, and not long afterwards the movement was originated by St. Bertrand in France. In the eleventh century hospitals were founded by William the Conqueror in Normandy. It was not, however, until the eighteenth century that any real attempt was made to educate or train the blind.

Pensions for the Blind
Valentine Hauy, who has been called "The father and apostle of the blind," spent his lifetime in furthering the interests of those afflicted with blindness.
In the early part of the nineteenth century the New England Blind Institute was organized and also the Massachusetts School for the Blind. William H. Prescott, the blind historian, was one of the organizers.
In Great Britain, the earliest legislation for the welfare of the blind was enacted in the days of Queen Elizabeth, but it was almost three hundred years later before a royal commission was appointed, in 1886, to investigate the conditions of the blind. This commission reported in 1889 and its report resulted in the passing of the Elementary Education Act in 1893. In 1914, as a result of a resolution in the House of Commons, a departmental committee was set up to investigate into the general welfare of the blind. In August, 1919, the Ministry of Health issued regulations and rules governing grants used out of public moneys to be distributed for the welfare of the blind In 1920, the Blind Persons Act was passed by which blind persons in Great Britain received the Old Age Pension at the age of fifty years instead of at the age of seventy years. In March, 1927, 14,562 persons in England and Wales were in receipt of a blind pension. Provision was also made for the education and care of the blind children, and, where possible, they were trained for remunerative employment.

Blind men and women throughout the ages have carved out for themselves important positions in the world. The story of the education and achievements of Laura Bridgman, who was deaf, dumb and blind, and of Helen Keller, and other deaf, blind mutes is known to almost everyone.
The world war gave a fresh impetus to the movement for the emancipation of the blind in every rank and walk of life, and it was largely instrumental in bringing to public attention the necessity for special recognition of those afflicted with blindness; and 92582-22

The number of blind people of which we have a record is enormous. Perhaps the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) with his fine memory would be able to quote these figures offhand. In England and Wales there are 46,822 blind people; in Scotland, 6,939; Northern Ireland, 1,758; in India there is the enormous total of 479,637 blind people; in Burma, 25,000; Austria, 5,359. In China blindness is very prevalent but government statistics are not available to show the total number of blind people there. Czechoslovakia has 5,000 blind people;

France, 29,000; Germany, 35,624; Japan, 100,000; Poland, 16,144, and the United States of America, 75,000.
The world's history furnishes the names of many blind people who became prominent in public and private affairs. John Stanley was born blind in 1713. He studied music and graduated as Music Bachelor at Oxford when sixteen years of age. He was a composer and received the degree of Doctor of Music, and was master of the King's band. Marie Paradis was born blind, but became famous as a pianist and vocalist. Doctor T. R. Armitage was born in 1824. He graduated in medicine and lost his sight at the age of thirty-six years. He afterwards devoted his life to the cause of the blind. Elizabeth Gilbert was born in 1826. She became blind at the age of three years, and devoted her whole life to the welfare of the blind. Sir Francis James Campbell, who was born in the state of Tennessee, became blind at the age of three years. He made many notable contributions to the cause of the blind. Henry Fawcett was accidentally blinded in his twenty-fifth year. He went to Cambridge university and became professor of political economy. He was elected as a member of the British House of Commons and later became Postmaster General of Great Britain. Doctor William Moon lost his sight in his early manhood. He made many contributions to the cause of the blind. Sir Arthur Pearson, the great newspaper magnate, who later became blind, left the stamp of his work for the blind throughout the British empire. He established the National Institute for the Blind in 1913-1914. No resume of famous blind people would be complete without mention of Fielding and John Milton. The latter ranks with Shakespeare in the writing of poetry and prose. Two of his most outstanding productions that will endure as long as the Anglo-Saxon tongue is spoken were Paradise Lost and Paradise Regained. These works were written after he became blind. Many of the famous musicians of the world were blind, two of the greatest being Bach and Handel, who became blind towards the end of their careers.
Coming more particularly to the position of the blind in Canada, our blind population, according to the records of the bureau of statistics, number about 6,350 people, though some estimates place it as high as 8,000. The total number of blind persons over the age of twenty-one years in Canada is 5,053. Within this classification, we find: mental defectives, 219; Indians, 73; old age pensioners, 221; workmen's compensation board blind, 47; mothers' allowance pensioners, 42; blinded

soldiers, 102. These groups are already recipients of financial assistance. In the seventy year and over classification, according to provinces, we find as follows: Prince Edward Island, 21; Nova Scotia, 104; New Brunswick, 57; Quebec, 289; Ontario, 527; Manitoba, 166; Saskatchewan, 147; Alberta, 66; British Columbia, 98; the total number of males blind being 767; females, 698-making a grand total of 1,465. For pensions estimates in this classification, there should be deducted: Indians, old age pensioners, workmen's compensation board cases, mothers' allowance pensioners and mental defectives, totalling in all 314. In the fifty to sixty-nine years classification: Prince Edward Island, 17; Nova Scotia, 112; New Brunswick, 82; Quebec, 293; Ontario, 711; Manitoba, 166; Saskatchewan, 136; Alberta, 56; British Columbia, 122; making a total number of males blind, 1,064; females, 631-making a grand total of 1,695.
