In the forty to forty-nine years classification: Prince Edward Island, 5; Nova Scotia, 68; New Brunswick, 27; Quebec, 138; Ontario, 305; Manitoba, 64; Saskatchewan, 68; Alberta, 33; British Columbia, 61; making a total male population of blind 537, and females, 233-or a grand total of 770. For pensions estimates, deduct Indians, mental defectives, mothers' allowance pensioners and blinded soldiers, totalling in all 108. For purposes of record, I shall also furnish an estimate of the number of blind in the various provinces between the ages of twenty-one and thirty-nine: Prince Edward Island, 13; Nova Scotia, 120; New Brunswick, 69; Quebec, 240; Ontario, 399; Manitoba, 103; Saskatchewan, 84; Alberta, 44; British Columbia, 51, making a total male population of 703 and a total female population of 420, or a grand total of 1,123. I have not prepared a classification of those under the age of twenty-one years who are afflicted with blindness.
Canada did little for her civilian blind population until the world war attracted her attention to the needs of the blind. No actual statistical records had been attempted up to that time. In 1916, however, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind was organized. They obtained a federal charter in 1918. which had for its object the amelioration of the conditions of the blind and the prevention of blindness. Federal grants covering administrative expenses only were received, while private contributions and provincial government grants were received to 92582-224
cover the practical work from the Atlantic to the Pacific and including Newfoundland.
Through the National Council for Child Welfare, the national institute locates blind infants and watches their development. Treatment at birth to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum is compulsory. Sight-saving classes have been started in several centres. Technical training as well as educational instruction is provided in Canadian schools for the blind. Training and institutional instruction is given to those who lose their sight between the ages of twenty-one and fifty years.
The Canadian National Institute for the Blind has for its patron His Excellency the Governor General of Canada, and many of the more prominent people in the public and social life of this country are associated in its activities from coast to coast. The work done on behalf of our blind by these organizations cannot be overestimated. The depression has taught us at least one useful lesson, that after all man is his brother's keeper.
In October, 1933, a united memorial was presented to the right honourable the Prime Minister of Canada by various organizations for aid and assistance to the blind. In that memorial reference was made to the fact that the underlying reasons which lead to the provision of pensions for the blind in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, and elsewhere were precisely the same as those that obtained in Canada. It was felt that voluntary contributions had steadily decreased during the period of the depression, with the result that the whole position of the blind population became accentuated. It was also pointed out that the provisions for general and unemployment relief funds deal only with cases from a destitution standpoint, and greater assistance is required to relieve the destitution of the blind than of persons with their sight; also, the whole problem is not a transient one, resulting from the present economic conditions, but is one of destitution arising from permanent unemployability. Voluntary agents are no longer able to meet the needs of the permanently unemployable adult blind, as sufficient private funds cannot be secured. Under the circumstances, it was pointed out to the government that the only adequate solution was the provision of a state pension or allowance. According to dispatches which appeared in the Toronto Mail and Empire on Saturday, June 30, 1934, the matter had been discussed before the dominion-provincial conference, having been introduced by the Prime Minister of Canada on the request of the National Institute for the Blind and the Canadian Federation for the

Pensions for the Blind
Blind. The conference itself was held in camera, and it was generally understood that Hon. Mr. Price, then Attorney-General of Ontario, was ready to implement any move that might be taken with a view to further aiding the blind pensioners. It was further stated that the whole matter would be reviewed with the improvement of the general financial situation.
We have in Canada many Canadians who have achieved great distinction in the various walks of life. I shall mention merely two, although there are many, many others. The late Trooper Lome Malloy, of Prescott, who was blinded during the South African war, later returned to this country, graduating with high honours in arts and law from Queens university. Later he took the law course at Osgoode Hall, Toronto, and practised law-in the county of Dundas. Mr. Phillip E. Layton, president of the Montreal Association for the Blind, is himself blind, and to-day he is recognized as one of Canada's greatest Canadians. Through his work and philanthropy he has done much to ameliorate the conditions of our blind.
I feel that the Prime Minister and all the members in all parts of the house are in sympathy with the subject matter of this resolution, and, in my humble opinion, the time has come when as a Christian nation we should give this deserving class of our citizens the benefit of state assistance. The courage and fortitude of those afflicted with blindness has been an amazing revelation to all those who from time to time come into contact with individual cases of blindness.

speechtext: T can say what I have to say in one minute. There is no time left to amplify my endorsement of this motion, but I wish to state that as mayor of Montreal I had many delegations coming to my office pressing for a measure of this kind. I have studied the matter and am quite willing to endorse the resolution. But I am not sure whether it would not be better to have separate legislation rather than link it with old age pensions. I take the motion to mean that provision similar to the old age pensions may be adopted for the blind. With that reservation I am in favour of the motion.

With the indulgence of the house, there is a matter to which I would like to allude for a moment. At times of adjournment there has been a certain amount of confusion. I think we can avoid that if we observe paragraph 5 of standing order 12, which states that:
When the house adjourns the members shall keep their seats until Mr. Speaker has left the chair.
As a general rule at the close of the sitting the leader of the government announces the program for the next day, if he fails to do so the leader of the opposition generally endeavours to get that information by question and answer, and at that time there is usually a certain amount of confusion. I know that
all hon. members are anxious to hear what the leader of the government has to say. Therefore I suggest that we 'bear this rule in mind at adjournment time so that the house may adjourn without confusion and with dignity and decorum.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put pursuant to standing order.
